title: Do this for a commemoration of me (Luke 22:14–20)
hookLine: Luke's words of institution, the root of the Mass

lines: THE WORDS SAID AT EVERY MASS.
cards: The words a priest says over the bread at every Mass were first spoken, Luke says, in an upper room in Jerusalem. Luke even tells how the room was found.
Jesus sends Peter and John ahead to prepare the Passover: follow a man carrying a pitcher of water into a house. The owner shows them a large upper room, furnished, just as Jesus said.
The hour comes, and he sits down at table with the twelve apostles.

teach.b: Luke begins with longing. Jesus says: "With desire I have desired to eat this pasch with you, before I suffer." The doubled phrase means: I have wanted this so much.
Then a detail Luke records: two cups. Early in the meal Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it; he won't drink again of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom comes.
Some readers connect this with the cups of wine at the Passover meal.

teach.h: THIS IS MY BODY, GIVEN FOR YOU.
teach.b: Then the bread: "And taking bread, he gave thanks, and brake; and gave to them, saying: This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me."

And after supper, the second cup: "This is the chalice, the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you." Commemoration, in the Greek, is anamnesis. It isn't nostalgia, like looking at an old photo.
The Passover command already speaks this way: Exodus tells each parent to explain the feast as what the Lord did for me, when I came out of Egypt. Remembering, there, makes the saving event present.
Catholics believe that at Mass the one sacrifice of Christ is made present, not repeated, and that the bread and wine become his body and blood, which the Church calls transubstantiation.

The Council of Trent also taught that with the words do this, Christ made the apostles priests. Other Christians understand these words differently; many Protestants see the supper as a memorial and a meal of faith.

teach.h: DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.
teach.b: All start from this same table and this same command. Not believe this, or understand this, first. Do this.

how: At every Mass the priest repeats the words of institution over the bread and wine, and Catholics kneel or bow at the elevation; on Holy Thursday the Church celebrates the Mass of the Lord's Supper, remembering this night.

o: a remembering that makes the past event present
the blessing said over a cup at a meal
a nostalgic memory, like an old photograph

games.q: the upper room — tap the pairs.
p: to eat this pasch with you

s: Luke's account mentions two cups at the supper
a cup before the bread (22:17) and the chalice after supper (22:20).
commemoration here means a nostalgic memory
anamnesis is remembering that makes the saving event present.
all Christians understand do this in exactly the same way
Catholics, Orthodox and many Protestants understand it differently, but all start from this table.

games.q: it's your last meal with your friends before you suffer. you take bread in your hands. what do you do first?
o: explain what's about to happen to you.
games.why: he gives thanks first, breaks the bread, and says this is my body, which is given for you. do this for a commemoration of me.

practice: Picture your next meal: the table, the plate, who'll be there, or that you'll be alone. Then picture, gently, that upper room: thirteen people, bread, a cup, a man who knew what was coming and still gave thanks.
If you pray, give thanks the way he did; if you don't, simply remember that night and the people at it.

wordCard.voice: Anamnesis. The Greek word behind commemoration in Jesus' command over the bread, the words of institution at the root of every Mass. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: remembrance, commemoration. In Catholic theology, the memorial that makes Christ's sacrifice present.

carryVoice: Your line: do this. A memory that makes the past present again. Good to see you today.
